title: "Will Islam Make You Cut Off Your Non-Muslim Friends?"
summary: Why declining alcohol, pork, and certain social settings doesn't mean withdrawing from non-Muslim relationships, and practical ways to stay socially connected as your habits change.

body.text: A very practical fear, not just an abstract one

Friends sometimes worry, sometimes aloud, that your new practice means the friendship is effectively over — no more shared drinks after work, no more casual meals together, an assumption that you're pulling away. This lesson is about addressing that directly, since it's one of the more immediate, everyday tensions many new Muslims face.

The concrete changes are narrower than they might seem: not drinking alcohol or eating pork yourself, and generally avoiding venues or events built specifically around those (a bar crawl, for instance). Being present at a gathering where others are eating or drinking those things, while you simply don't partake, is a completely normal, common arrangement most new Muslims settle into without dropping the relationship or the invitation.
Islamic teaching actively encourages maintaining good relationships

As covered in the Social Dealings lesson, kindness toward neighbours, friends, and colleagues — regardless of their faith — is a direct, repeated Islamic teaching, not something in tension with practising the religion seriously. Withdrawing from all non-Muslim friendships isn't a marker of stronger faith; if anything, maintaining good character and kindness across those relationships is presented as part of faithful practice.

body.translation: Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion... from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them.

body.text: Many new Muslims find it works well to suggest alternative shared activities (a coffee instead of a bar, a daytime outing instead of an evening built around drinking), be upfront and matter-of-fact about the change rather than avoiding the topic, and simply keep showing up where you comfortably can. Friendships that are genuinely valued on both sides tend to adapt; the change reveals which relationships were built on more than the specific activities involved, which can be a hard but clarifying realisation either way.

body.question: Is it okay to just sit with friends at a bar without drinking myself?
body.answer: Many scholars distinguish between merely being present in a venue where others are drinking (generally considered acceptable, especially briefly or for a specific social reason) and actively participating in or normalising the activity — if the environment itself feels genuinely uncomfortable or tempting for you personally, it's completely fine to suggest a different setting instead, without needing to frame it as a moral objection to your friends.

body.question: What if a friend takes real offence at the change?
body.answer: Give it time and stay warm rather than immediately assuming the friendship is over — genuine friendships often adjust once the initial surprise passes, especially if you keep the relationship active through other shared activities rather than letting distance build by default.

body.question: Is there a specific friendship where this change has already come up, or that you're anticipating navigating? What's one alternative activity you could suggest?
